St Austell.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Cornish clay country
s1loc: St Austell anchors one of Cornwall's biggest visitor draws in the Eden Project, the Grimshaw-designed biomes built into a reclaimed china clay pit at Bodelva, where the Rainforest and Mediterranean domes pull crowds across the season. The Wheal Martyn China Clay Museum at Carthew tells the kaolin story on a working Victorian site, while the Georgian port of Charlestown, a film and Poldark location, gives St Austell Bay a heritage waterfront of tall ships and harbour walls.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the coast and the old clay tips, with Carlyon Bay and Porthpean beaches offering paddleboard hire and bathing, and the nine off-road Clay Trails linking the clay villages for walking and cycling. Pinetum Park and Pine Lodge Gardens at Holmbush, the Black Gold cinema and St Austell Leisure Centre add to the family offer, with the Cornish Coast Path and Par Sands a short ride away through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture centre on the St Austell Brewery Visitor Centre on Trevarthian Road, telling over 150 years of brewing, and the Austell Project sculptures including the fourteen-metre Earth Goddess that mark the town's clay roots. Holy Trinity Church with its sixteenth-century tower, the Italianate Town Hall and Market House on Fore Street, and the Lost Gardens of Heligan at Pentewan carry the events and garden calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base led by the Carlyon Bay Hotel and Spa above the bay, with guesthouses and self-catering across Charlestown and Carlyon, and a guide scene built on Eden, clay-trail and coast tours. St Austell station on the Cornish Main Line runs direct to Plymouth and London Paddington, while the A390, the A30 and Newquay Airport carry day-trippers out toward Truro, Newquay and Bodmin across the season.

Consett.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north-west Durham
s1loc: Consett anchors its visitor draw on the Hownsgill Viaduct, Thomas Bouch's towering 1858 railway bridge above the Hownsgill valley, now a footpath and cycleway on the C2C coast-to-coast route. The town's steel-town past survives in the Project Genesis heritage trail, the surviving steelworks pumphouse and the public art that marks the old works, with Consett Urban Park and the open moorland above the Derwent valley pulling walkers and cyclists across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the river paths, with Allensford Country Park offering riverside walks, picnic lawns and play beside the Derwent, and Derwent Waterside Park giving fishing, sailing and trails. The Waskerley Way and Lanchester Valley railway paths strike out from the town toward Stanhope and Durham, while the Grove Ponds and Fawcett Park give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Empire Theatre and Cinema on Front Street, a restored venue hosting live shows and films, and the nearby world-class draws of Beamish, the Living Museum of the North at Stanley, and the Tanfield Railway with the 1725 Causey Arch, the oldest railway bridge in the world. The coke-oven remnants, the Project Genesis trail and the town's events calendar carry visitors through the year across north-west Durham.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the north-west Durham and Derwent valley visitor area, with a guide scene built on C2C cycle trips and steel-heritage walks. The A691, A692 and A68 carry day-trippers in across the Pennine fringe, while Durham and Chester-le-Street stations and the wider Tyneside network draw weekend crowds out from Stanley, Chester-le-Street and Gateshead across the season.

Newton Aycliffe.region: Newton Aycliffe and the Vale of Durham
Newton Aycliffe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of Durham
s1loc: Newton Aycliffe sits in the cradle of the railways, with the Hitachi Rail factory at Merchant Park on Aycliffe Business Park building trains beside the line where the Stockton and Darlington Railway first ran in 1825. Locomotion at Shildon, part of the National Railway Museum, displays Locomotion No. 1 and a great hall of historic engines a short ride away, giving the town a marquee railway-heritage draw across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs through West Park, with its boating lake, sculpture trail, landscaped gardens and playground, and the Great Aycliffe Way, a scenic walking and cycling ring encircling the town through woodlands and meadows. Aycliffe Nature Park, with its pond, wetland and birdlife, and the two-mile Locomotion Way linking Shildon and Newton Aycliffe give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture centre on Bishop Auckland's Auckland Project nearby, with Auckland Tower, Auckland Palace, the Mining Art Gallery, the Spanish Gallery, the Walled Garden and the Deer Park drawing visitors through the year. Raby Castle at Staindrop, a complete medieval fortress with deer park, walled gardens and tearoom, and the seasonal festivals and reenactments across the Vale carry the events calendar through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel base led by Redworth Hall Hotel in its parkland estate, with inns and guesthouses serving the Vale of Durham, and a guide scene built on Railway 200, Locomotion and castle tours. Newton Aycliffe station runs services to Darlington, Bishop Auckland and Middlesbrough, while the A1(M) and Darlington's East Coast Main Line carry day-trippers out toward Darlington, Bishop Auckland and Spennymoor across the season.

Thornaby-on-Tees.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Teesside
s1loc: Thornaby-on-Tees sits on the south bank of the river opposite Stockton, with the Tees Heritage Park stretching along the water between Stockton and Yarm its marquee green draw, threaded by the Teesdale Way and the Thornaby Trail. Norman St Peter's Church on Thornaby Green, the former airfield streets named for RAF aircraft and stations, and the Riverside path give the town a genuine heritage and waterside pull across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Teesside Park, the riverside retail and leisure complex with cinema, bowling and dining, and Bassleton Wood and The Holmes, a horseshoe of woodland and grassland within a great bend of the Tees. Village Park with its bowling club and outdoor fitness, the River Banks running route and the cycleways toward Preston Park and Ingleby Barwick give families and activity operators a steady outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run across the river to Preston Park Museum and Grounds, the Victorian mansion at Eaglescliffe with its recreated 1895 street, and the restored Art Deco Stockton Globe, a 3,000-capacity music and comedy venue. The Stockton International Riverside Festival on the new Waterfront, Stockton Calling and the events at the Globe, a short walk from Thornaby station, carry the cultural calendar through the year across Teesside.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving the wider Teesside and Tees Valley visitor area, with a guide scene built on river-heritage and railway-birthplace tours. Thornaby station runs frequent services across the Tees Valley line, while the A19, the A66 and Teesside International Airport carry day-trippers out toward Stockton-on-Tees, Middlesbrough and Billingham across the season.

Portishead.region: Portishead and the North Somerset coast
Portishead.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the North Somerset coast
s1loc: Portishead anchors its visitor economy on its modern Marina, a 250-berth harbour ringed by tiered waterfront homes, cafes, bars and the Portishead Public Art Trail that traces the town's maritime past. The Lake Grounds on the seafront, with its traditional boating lake, pedalos, rose garden and cricket pitch, and the community-run heated open-air pool with its Cafe Lido give the town a classic coastal draw across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the estuary, with Portishead Sailing Club off Sugar Loaf Beach and the Portishead Coastal Path winding toward Clevedon with its Grade I-listed Victorian pier. The Portbury Wharf Nature Reserve, a 113-acre site of wetland, woodland and bird hides for swans, herons and warblers, and the open lawns and tennis of the Lake Grounds give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Portishead's restored quay, the public sculptures of the marina trail and the Royal Inn and waterside dining around the harbour, with the Grade I Clevedon Pier and Victorian Clevedon a short coast walk away. The National Trust's Victorian Gothic Tyntesfield estate at Wraxall, fifteen minutes inland, and the town's seafront events carry visitors through the year along the North Somerset coast.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the Bristol and North Somerset visitor area, with a guide scene built on marina, coast-path and nature-reserve tours. The M5 at junctions 19 and 20, the A369 to Bristol and the Portway carry day-trippers in, while Bristol's rail and Bristol Airport draw weekend crowds out toward Clevedon, Bristol and Weston-super-Mare across the season.

Ferndown.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Dorset
s1loc: Ferndown sits between two great heaths north of Bournemouth, with Moors Valley Country Park and Forest at Ashley Heath its marquee draw, an 800-acre Forestry England and Dorset Council site drawing over 750,000 visitors a year. The narrow-gauge steam railway, the Go Ape high ropes, the Tree Top Trail, the Gruffalo sculpture trail and the adventure golf and play areas give the town a major family attraction on its doorstep across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across the heaths and woods, with Holt Heath National Nature Reserve and Avon Heath Country Park giving heathland walks, wildlife and all of Britain's native reptiles, and cycle hire threading the Dorset woodlands. The three premier golf clubs of Ferndown, Broadstone and Parkstone, and the wider trails toward Wimborne Minster give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the season.

Heritage and culture run through Ferndown's horticultural roots, where the Stewart family opened one of Britain's first garden retail nurseries in 1955, having grown plants on the warm heath from 1864. The National Trust's Kingston Lacy at Wimborne, a grand country house with art collection, Japanese garden, ornamental lakes and parkland, and the events at Moors Valley carry visitors through the year across east Dorset.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, inn and guesthouse trade serving the Bournemouth, Poole and east Dorset visitor area, with a guide scene built on country-park, heath and garden tours. The A31 and the A348 Ringwood Road carry day-trippers in, while Bournemouth's seafront, the South West Main Line and Bournemouth Airport draw weekend crowds out toward Bournemouth, Poole and Christchurch across the season.

Broadstairs.region: Broadstairs and the Isle of Thanet
Broadstairs.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Isle of Thanet
s1loc: Broadstairs runs a busy seaside visitor economy built on Viking Bay, the sheltered sandy cove below the old town with its tidal pool, traditional promenade and harbour, set among a necklace of seven chalk-cliff bays. Bleak House on the cliff top, where Charles Dickens holidayed and wrote, and the Dickens House Museum on Victoria Parade, former home of the model for Betsey Trotwood, give the town a marquee literary draw across the warmer season.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the bays, with Botany Bay and its chalk stacks, Stone Bay, Joss Bay for surfing and Louisa Bay strung along the coast for bathing, paddleboarding and rock-pooling. The Viking Coastal Trail for walkers and cyclists, the Memorial Recreation Ground and the wide sands at low tide give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer through the season on the Thanet coast.

Heritage and culture centre on the Crampton Tower Museum, the flint tower dedicated to Victorian railway engineer Thomas Crampton, the annual Broadstairs Dickens Festival each June with its costumed parades, and the international Broadstairs Folk Week each August. The old harbour, the York Gate arch, the Victorian villas and the town's full events calendar carry visitors through the year across the Isle of Thanet.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, guesthouse and Bed and Breakfast trade serving the Thanet coast, with a guide scene built on Dickens, bay and clifftop tours, and the wider draws of Margate's Turner Contemporary and Dreamland and Ramsgate's Royal Harbour nearby. Broadstairs station on the Kent Coast line and the High Speed services to London St Pancras, with the A256 and Quex Park at Birchington, carry day-trippers out toward Ramsgate, Margate and Herne Bay across the season.
